Guru Amar Das

Stories of the Sikh Gurus

Guru Amar Das

The Guru of Service

In everyday English — the whole story of the third Guru

Stories by Eku

How to Read · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read it out loud. This story was made to be told. Read slowly, as if you were sitting among family at home — with the smell of the langar and the sound of the Beas river in the background.

The yellow boxes are the characters speaking in their own words. Change your voice a little when you read them — Amar Das's slow and humble, Angad's grave, Datu's angry.

(The purple cues) tell you where to pause, whisper, or raise your voice. They are for the reader, not the listener.

At the end of every part, the green box — Pause and think. Stop there. Ask questions. Let the listener speak. In this story, those questions matter as much as the story.

There are two kinds of things in this book — Amar Das's own bani, written in the Guru Granth Sahib, and the stories of the tradition, told in the sangat for centuries. Where a story comes from the tradition, the book says so plainly — 'the tradition tells us'. Where the words are Amar Das's own, the book names them.

This book's main story comes from Amar Das's bani and the traditional life stories. The full list of sources is at the end of the book.

Who's Who · · WHO'S WHO

Guru Amar Das — the heart of this story. Born in Basarke, a disciple of Guru Angad at sixty, twelve years of service, and the third Guru at seventy-three. The Guru of service.

Tej Bhan — Amar Das's father. A Bhalla Khatri of Basarke, a farmer and a trader.

Bakht Kaur — Amar Das's mother. The old writings also call her Lachmi and Rup Kaur.

Mansa Devi — Amar Das's wife, the daughter of Devi Chand of Sankhatra.

Mohan and Mohri — Amar Das's two sons. Dani and Bhani — his two daughters. Bhani was married to Bhai Jetha.

Bibi Amro — Guru Angad's daughter. It was her song that brought Amar Das to the Guru's door. She was married to Amar Das's nephew.

Guru Angad — the second Guru of the Sikhs. He lived at Khadur; Amar Das served him for twelve years.

Baba Buddha — the oldest and most revered Sikh. He had been in the sangat since Nanak's time; it was he who applied the tilak to Amar Das.

Bhai Jetha — Amar Das's son-in-law, Bhani's husband. Amar Das made him his successor — and he became known as Guru Ram Das.

Datu — Guru Angad's son. He believed the guruship should have been his.

Akbar — the emperor of India. The tradition says he came to Goindwal and ate in the langar.

Goinda — a Marwaha Khatri trader, whose plan founded the village of Goindwal.

1 · Birth — Basarke · · BIRTH — BASARKE

Not far from Amritsar, on the plain of Punjab, there was a village — Basarke. There, in the year 1479, on Baisakh Sudi 14, Samvat 1536 — 5 May 1479 — a child was born whose name was Amar Das.

The child's father, Tej Bhan, was a Bhalla Khatri — he farmed and traded. His mother, Bakht Kaur, kept the home. Amar Das was the eldest son of the house — three more brothers came after him.

Amar Das was religious from childhood. He rose in the morning to pray, served holy men, and was always ready to help the people of the village. When he grew up, he married Mansa Devi — the daughter of Devi Chand of Sankhatra village. They had four children — two sons, Mohan and Mohri, and two daughters, Dani and Bhani.

There was a home, fields, trade, a family. From the outside, Amar Das's life looked like the life of an ordinary, honest householder. But inside him there was a restlessness — a question that stayed with him for years — what is the way to God? Is pilgrimage and prayer the only way — or is there another way too?

He found the answer to that question at the age of sixty. But before that, he took the path that the Hindu devotees of his time took — the yearly pilgrimage to bathe in the Ganges.

The date of birth — one question

Most sources (the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism and modern scholars) say Amar Das was born on 5 May 1479 at Basarke. But some old writings also give the birth year as 1509. This book follows 1479 in the main story, because it is the reckoning under which all the other milestones of his life fit together — meeting Angad in 1540, the guruship in 1552, death in 1574.

His mother's name — three names, one mother

Amar Das's mother's name is written differently in the old writings — Bakht Kaur, Lachmi and Rup Kaur. These are three names of the same person, as recorded in the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism. This book uses Bakht Kaur in the main story.

Pause and think — Amar Das had everything — a home, fields, trade, a family. Yet there was a question in his heart that gave him no rest. Has a question like that ever come to your heart — one whose answer you still have not found?

2 · Twenty Pilgrimages · · TWENTY PILGRIMAGES

Amar Das was a Vaishnav devotee — a devotee of Vishnu, who went every year to Haridwar to bathe in the Ganges. The old writings say he made twenty such pilgrimages — twenty years, twenty baths in the Ganges.

Every journey was the same — walking on foot, meeting holy men on the way, taking a dip in the Ganges, and holding in his heart the faith that this was how God would be found. Amar Das did it with his whole heart. He was no show-off devotee — he was truly searching for God.

Then, returning from the twentieth journey, something happened. On the way he met a sadhu. The sadhu looked at Amar Das — white beard, tilak, rosary — and said — you have bathed in the Ganges for so many years, but you have no Guru? Without a Guru, what use is all this?

The tradition says the sadhu's words pierced Amar Das's heart. He made a vow in his mind — now I must have a Guru. Without a Guru, pilgrimage and prayer are all incomplete.

Amar Das returned home. But his heart was no longer the same as before. He had been to the Ganges twenty times. Now he wanted what he had not found in the Ganges — a Guru, who would show him the way to God.

Twenty journeys — the tradition's count

The count of twenty pilgrimages comes from the old chronicles — the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism gives the same count. The sadhu's rebuke is also the tradition's story. This book keeps it here because it was the turning point that changed Amar Das's life.

Pause and think — The sadhu said — without a Guru, what use is all this? Do you think a teacher is needed to learn something — or can a person learn alone? And who are the teachers in your life?

3 · Meeting Guru Angad — Twelve Years of Seva · · MEETING GURU ANGAD — TWELVE YEARS OF SEVA

There was a young woman connected to Amar Das's family — Bibi Amro. She was Guru Angad's daughter, and she was married to Amar Das's nephew. When Amar Das went to meet her, he heard something he had never heard before.

Amro was singing Guru Nanak's bani early in the morning — in a calm, sweet voice, as if someone were speaking from the heart. Amar Das stopped still. He had been to the Ganges twenty times, he had heard many hymns — but there was something else in this song. There was no fear in it, no show — only a simple truth: God is near, and the Name is the way.

Amar Das asked — daughter, whose song is this? Amro said — this is the bani of Guru Nanak, who was my father Guru Angad's Guru. My father lives at Khadur — he is the one who knows it.

Amar Das said — take me to your father. Amro took him to Khadur — where Guru Angad lived. It was the year 1540, and Amar Das was about sixty years old.

When Amar Das reached Khadur and saw Guru Angad, he became his disciple without another word. At sixty years of age, after twenty pilgrimages, Amar Das had found what he had been searching for — a Guru.

Pause and think — One song changed Amar Das's life. Has it ever happened to you that a song, a sentence, or a book changed the way you think? What was it?

After becoming Angad's disciple, Amar Das changed his whole life. He stayed on at Khadur. And for the next twelve years — from 1540 to 1552 — he did one thing — seva, service.

He rose three hours before dawn — while the village was still asleep. Then he fetched water from the Beas river for the Guru's bath. In the daytime he worked in the langar — cooking food, serving it, washing the vessels. When he had time, he brought firewood from the forest — for the Guru's langar. Morning and evening he meditated on the Name and sat in kirtan.

The tradition says that one stormy night Amar Das went for water even then — fierce wind, rain, lightning. On the way, near the weavers' colony, he struck a peg and fell. He was hurt — but the pitcher on his head did not fall. Not a single drop of water spilled.

A weaver woman's sleep was broken. She said in annoyance — this is 'Amaru Nithavan' — Amaru the homeless, who has no home. When this reached Guru Angad, he said — yes, Amar Das is the home of the homeless, the support of the unsupported, the strength of the weak, and the one who shows the way to those who are lost.

For twelve years Amar Das did this — no complaint, no demand. He was a sixty-year-old man, yet in service he was less than no young man. Everyone in the sangat knew — if the Guru has one most humble servant, it is Amar Das.

Guru Angad watched. He knew to whom the guruship would go. The guruship does not go to a son — it goes to the one who proves himself in service.

What did Amro sing?

The different tellings of the tradition name Amro's song differently — some say she was singing the Japji, some say the first verse of the Anand Sahib ('Anand bhaya meri mae'). This book does not name the song in the main story — it says only that she was singing Guru Nanak's bani, because both tellings are the tradition's, and in both the heart of it is the same.

1539 or 1540?

The sources differ slightly on the date of the meeting with Angad — some say 1539, some 1540 (Samvat 1597). This book follows 1540 in the main story, which is the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism's reckoning — and it is also the reckoning from which twelve years of service lead to the guruship of 1552.

The stormy night — the tradition's story

The stormy night, the fetching of water, and the weaver woman calling him 'Amaru Nithavan' is a sakhi of the tradition — told in the Janamsakhi and Gurbilas stories. Angad's words — 'home of the homeless, support of the unsupported' — are in that same story. The twelve years of service, rising before dawn, fetching water from the Beas, and working in the langar are also recorded in the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism.

Pause and think — Amar Das was sixty years old — and still he rose first every morning. Does service have an age? And is the one who serves ever small — or is it service itself that makes a person great?

4 · Guru at Seventy-Three · · GURU AT SEVENTY-THREE

The year 1552 came. Guru Angad's health was failing. He called his disciples and said — the time has come to hand over the guruship.

Everyone in the sangat looked to Angad's sons. But Angad called Amar Das to him. The tradition says that Baba Buddha applied the tilak to his forehead, and Angad handed him the guruship with the offering of a coconut and five paise. In March 1552, at the age of seventy-three, Amar Das became the third Guru of the Sikhs.

Guru Angad died on 29 March 1552 — at the age of 48. The sangat saw it — the Guru had changed, but the light was the same. As one lamp lights another — the flame stays the same, the lamp changes.

Amar Das took up the guruship — but there was a difficulty before him. Angad's sons were not happy with this decision. They believed the guruship should have been theirs. To avoid a quarrel, Amar Das left Khadur for Goindwal — on the bank of the Beas river, on the Delhi–Lahore road, near an important ferry crossing.

The foundation of Goindwal had been laid at Guru Angad's own bidding — from the plan of a trader named Goinda. Now that same Goindwal became Amar Das's home — and the new centre of the Sikh Panth.

The date of the guruship — March 1552

The sources differ on the day — some say 26 March 1552, some 16 April 1552. The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism says Angad made Amar Das his successor in March 1552, before his death. This book says 'March 1552' in the main story, and both dates are recorded here in this note.

Baba Buddha — the one who applied the tilak

Baba Buddha was a Sikh from Nanak's time — he was regarded as the oldest and most revered person in the sangat. The tradition says it was he who applied the tilak to Amar Das, just as he later applied it to Guru Ram Das and Guru Arjan as well.

Pause and think — The guruship went not to a son, but to a sixty-year-old servant — who became Guru at seventy-three. Is there a right age to become a leader? And does leadership come from blood — or from service?

5 · Goindwal and the Baoli Sahib · · GOINDWAL AND THE BAOLI SAHIB

Goindwal stood on the bank of the Beas river — on the road from Delhi to Lahore, near a great ferry crossing. Travellers came and went here, traders stopped here, and now — the Guru's court was here too. Amar Das made Goindwal the main seat of the Sikhs.

In 1559, Amar Das began building a baoli at Goindwal — a stepped well, with stairs going down to the water. The sangat dug it together — Baba Buddha was with them. When the baoli was ready, people came from far and near — to bathe, to meditate on the Name, and to see the Guru.

The tradition says the baoli has eighty-four steps — a symbol of release from the cycle of eighty-four lakh births. The devotee who walks down, meditating on the Name at every step, purifies his own heart. Even today, people walk down those same steps at the Baoli Sahib.

Amar Das made Goindwal not just a village, but a place of pilgrimage. He fixed three gatherings of the year, when Sikhs would come together at Goindwal — at Baisakhi, at Maghi, and at Diwali. The sangat from far away came on those days — and the Guru's court became like a fair.

And it was at Goindwal that Amar Das did the work that became his greatest mark — the rule of the langar, whose story is in the next part.

Eighty-four steps — the tradition's telling

The eighty-four steps of the baoli is the tradition's telling — a symbol of release from the eighty-four lakh births. The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism says that once the baoli was ready, pilgrims came from far and near, and Goindwal was named by its founder as the Sikhs' first place of pilgrimage. The baoli was begun in 1559. Today it is reached by a covered passage of steps.

Kurukshetra — one firm date

One date in Amar Das's life is regarded as firm from the Guru Granth Sahib itself — his visit to Kurukshetra at the time of the abhijit nakshatra, which modern scholars' calculations place on 14 January 1553. It is one of the strongest dates in this book.

Pause and think — Every devotee who walks down into the baoli meditates on the Name at every step. Is there a 'step' like that in your life — some small thing you do every day that makes your heart quiet?

6 · Langar and Pangat · · LANGAR AND PANGAT

At Goindwal, Amar Das made a rule that is still the mark of every gurdwara today — pahile pangat pachhe sangat — first the row, then the congregation. That is: whoever came to meet the Guru had first to sit in the langar and eat — and only then would they have the Guru's darshan.

In the langar there was no great and no small. King or poor man, Hindu or Muslim, high caste or low — all sat in a single row and ate the same food. In those days this was no small thing — it was a revolution. The walls of caste and rank fell in the pangat of the langar.

The langar stayed open day and night. Travellers, beggars, strangers — whoever came, got food. Whatever was left was given to the cattle and the birds — nothing was wasted. And every day a sweet dish was also cooked in the langar — prasad, which later became the Sikhs' sacred prasad.

The tradition says that one day the emperor of India, Akbar, came to Goindwal. There was a stir in the sangat — the emperor is coming! Should special arrangements be made for him? Amar Das said — no special arrangements. The emperor is like everyone else. The Guru's door is open to all — king and subject, Hindu and Muslim, rich and poor, all are equal.

The tradition says Akbar sat in the langar among ordinary people and ate the simple food. He was so impressed by the working of the langar that he offered land for it. Amar Das said — emperor, thank you for your kindness. But the Guru's langar runs on the sangat's honest work — not on a king's grant. The Sikh is the one who earns and shares.

Akbar's visit — the tradition's story

The story of Akbar's visit to Goindwal is the tradition's — it is found in later granths such as the Mahima Prakash, and there is no contemporary record of it. So history cannot fix this visit firmly in place. The tradition gives the year of the visit as 1569 — some tellings also give 1560. This book tells it as the tradition's story, and says so plainly here. The offer of land and the Guru's refusal are part of that same tradition.

Pahile pangat pachhe sangat

The rule of eating in the langar first — 'pahile pangat pachhe sangat' — was Amar Das's command, recorded in the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism. The langar itself was begun by Guru Nanak at Kartarpur; Amar Das made it a condition for meeting the Guru, and so made its equality even firmer.

Pause and think — Even the emperor sat in the langar among ordinary people. Which places around you are there where everyone sits together — and which places still run on 'great and small'?

7 · Anand Karaj and the Dignity of Women · · ANAND KARAJ AND THE DIGNITY OF WOMEN

◆ This part is not for younger listeners

Amar Das wrote a song in his bani — the Anand Sahib, also called Anandu. In Raag Ramkali, a song of forty stanzas, it is a song of anand — of bliss. Its first verse is —

Anand bhaya meri mae, satguru mai paaya.

It means — bliss has come, O mother, for I have found the True Guru. This song came to be sung at weddings, at births, and on every happy occasion — and from it came the foundation of the Sikh marriage tradition, the Anand Karaj — the work of bliss, the joyful wedding.

In Amar Das's time, the condition of women was not good. There was a custom called sati — in which, on her husband's death, the wife was made to burn with him on his funeral pyre. Amar Das spoke plainly against it — this is not a custom, it is cruelty. A woman's life does not end with her husband's death. He said a widow may marry again — her life has as much right as anyone else's.

Amar Das also opposed purdah — the veil over the face. He said a woman has no need to hide; she may sit as an equal in the sangat, sing bani, and take part in the Guru's work. He also gave women charge of looking after sangats in some places — so women too could lead the Guru's work.

Amar Das also broke the divisions of caste — he said people of different castes may marry one another, because a marriage is the meeting of two souls, not of two castes. And he also spoke for living with one wife — monogamy.

Saying all this was not easy in those days. But Amar Das said — a faith that thinks women small is an incomplete faith. Before God, woman and man are equal.

Anand Karaj — Amar Das's foundation, Ram Das's Lavan

The Sikh marriage, the Anand Karaj, is rooted in Amar Das's Anand Sahib (Anandu, 40 stanzas, Raag Ramkali) — the song came to be sung at weddings and on every religious occasion. The four Lavan read at weddings are not Amar Das's — they are the composition of his successor, Guru Ram Das. This book keeps that difference plain.

Sati and purdah — what the Guru said

Speaking against sati, supporting widow remarriage, opposing purdah, and giving women charge of sangats — all of this is recorded in the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism as Amar Das's work. Note this — Amar Das gave a religious teaching against sati; it was not a king's law. That is why this part carries the mark at the top saying it is not for younger listeners — the matter of sati is not for them.

Pause and think — Amar Das said — a faith that thinks women small is incomplete. Which differences between women and men are still around you today — and which ones still need to change?

8 · The Manji — Twenty-Two Centres · · THE MANJI — TWENTY-TWO CENTRES

The sangat at Goindwal kept growing — people came from Punjab, from Delhi, from far away. Amar Das thought — if everyone must come to Goindwal, how will the far-off people stay connected? How will the Guru's message reach every village?

He made a new arrangement — the Manji system. He divided the Sikh sangat's area into twenty-two manjis — twenty-two centres, from Punjab to Bengal and Delhi. At each manji he placed a trusted Sikh, who sang bani to the sangat there, spread the Guru's message, looked after the sangat, and sent the sangat's offerings to Goindwal.

'Manji' means a cot — the cot on which the preacher sat to teach. The one who sat on the manji was no priest — he was an ordinary, trusted Sikh, chosen by the Guru. In this way the Guru's work was no longer only at Goindwal — it spread across the whole of India.

Amar Das did one more great work — he began gathering the bani of the earlier Gurus and the words of the bhagats into pothis, books. Those pothis later became the foundation of the Adi Granth — today's Guru Granth Sahib.

The Manji system gave the Sikh Panth a structure — an arrangement in which even the far-off Sikh stayed joined to the Guru. Scholars say this was the time when the Sikh sangat began to grow from a community into an organised Panth.

Twenty-two manjis — what is firm

The number of twenty-two manjis and their work — preaching, looking after the sangat, sending offerings — is recorded in the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism. Giving women charge of sangats in some sectors is recorded there too — it is called the Piri system. The old writings differ on the full list of the manjis and their regions, so this book gives no full list.

The pothis — the first step towards the Adi Granth

Amar Das gathered the bani of the earlier Gurus and the bhagats into pothis — this is recorded in the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism, and it is regarded as the first step towards the later Adi Granth.

Pause and think — The one who sat on the manji was no priest — he was an ordinary Sikh chosen by the Guru. Do you think the work of faith belongs only to priests — or to every person?

9 · Datu's Opposition · · DATU'S OPPOSITION

Amar Das's work at Goindwal was growing — but at Khadur there was a man who could not bear it — Datu, Guru Angad's son.

After his father's death, Datu had declared himself Guru. He believed the guruship belonged to the son — and Amar Das was only the man who used to fetch water in their house. He came to Goindwal with some of his supporters and said to Amar Das, seated on the Guru's seat — only yesterday you were fetching water in our house, and today you sit as Guru?

The tradition says that in his anger Datu kicked Amar Das — so hard that the old Guru fell from his seat. Then Datu sat on the seat himself and said — now I am the Guru.

Amar Das rose. He showed no anger, he said nothing to Datu. The tradition says he stroked Datu's foot and said — your tender foot must be hurt by my old, hard bones. Then he quietly left Goindwal — without any quarrel, without any complaint.

For some time Amar Das stayed away from Goindwal. The sangat grew worried — where is the Guru? Then Baba Buddha persuaded him and brought him back. Datu too slowly stepped back — and the sangat understood that the guruship is not won by a kick; it is won by service.

Datu's story — the tradition's story

Datu declaring himself Guru, coming to Goindwal and kicking Amar Das, and Amar Das stroking his foot — all of this is the tradition's story, told in the Gurbilas and the old writings. Amar Das leaving Goindwal and Baba Buddha bringing him back is part of that same tradition. This book tells it without exaggeration, naming the kick in a single line — and no violence is shown in it.

Pause and think — Datu kicked him — and Amar Das stroked his foot. Do you think anger should be answered with anger — or with calm? And is calm a weakness — or the greatest strength?

10 · The Successor — Bhai Jetha · · THE SUCCESSOR — BHAI JETHA

The year 1574 came. Amar Das was ninety-five years old. He had been Guru for twenty-two years — he had founded Goindwal, built the baoli, made the manjis, opened the langar to all, and spoken for the dignity of women. Now it was time to hand over the guruship.

The same question rose in the sangat — to whom will the guruship go? Amar Das had his own sons — Mohan and Mohri. But Amar Das did what Nanak and Angad had done — the guruship was decided not by blood, but by service.

Amar Das called his son-in-law — the husband of his daughter Bhani — Bhai Jetha. Jetha had served the Guru for years — he worked at Goindwal, served in the langar, and had made a place in the sangat's heart. Amar Das placed his hand on his head and said — from today your name is Ram Das. You will be the Guru after me.

On 1 September 1574, Guru Amar Das died at Goindwal — at the age of 95. The sangat saw it — the Guru had changed, but the light was the same. As one lamp lights another — the flame stays the same, the lamp changes.

After Amar Das, Guru Ram Das took up the sangat. He founded a new town — Ramdaspur, which today is called Amritsar — and had a sarovar dug there. But that is the story of the next book.

The date of death — 1 September 1574

Amar Das died on 1 September 1574 (Bhadon Sudi 14, Samvat 1631) at Goindwal — this date is recorded in the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism. His age is taken as 95 years.

Jetha — a son-in-law, not a son

Amar Das passed over his sons Mohan and Mohri and made his son-in-law Bhai Jetha his successor. Scholars hold different views on this — some see it as the beginning of a family tradition in the guruship, some as a decision of service and merit. This book says only that the decision was made by service — as in the time of Nanak and Angad.

Pause and think — Amar Das gave the guruship not to his sons, but to his son-in-law — who had served for years. Is the right leader the one who comes from the family — or the one who comes from service?

To Think About · · TO THINK ABOUT

Amar Das's story is no king's story, no warrior's story. It is the story of a man who became a disciple at sixty, fetched water for twelve years, became Guru at seventy-three — and then remained Guru for twenty-two years.

His message fits into a single word — seva, service. Service is devotion. The one who serves others serves God. Amar Das raised no sword, asked for no throne — he only served, and from service alone he raised a Panth.

Amar Das taught that to become a Guru you do not need youth, or strength, or family — you need only one thing — humility. The one who can rise before dawn and fetch water for others — he can become a Guru.

And the greatest thing — Amar Das said that before God all are equal. In the pangat of the langar, even the emperor is an ordinary man. In the sangat, even a woman is a leader. In a marriage, it is not caste that meets, but two souls.

Amar Das's own bani is in the Guru Granth Sahib to this day — 907 shabads. The greatest of them is the Anand Sahib — the song of bliss, sung in every Sikh home.

After Amar Das came seven more Gurus — Ram Das, Arjan, Hargobind, Har Rai, Har Krishan, Tegh Bahadur, and Gobind Singh. And in the end that light merged into the Guru Granth Sahib — which is the Sikhs' Guru to this day. Their stories will come in the next books of this series.

But this third book ends here — at Goindwal, on the bank of the Beas river, with a question — if Amar Das were here today, what would he say in your home, in your city? Perhaps just this — serve, share what you eat, and hold everyone equal.

Where This Story Comes From · · WHERE THIS STORY COMES FROM

The main source — Amar Das's own bani

The firmest foundation of this book is Guru Amar Das's own bani, recorded in the Guru Granth Sahib — 907 shabads. The greatest of them is the Anand Sahib (Anandu) — in Raag Ramkali, a song of forty stanzas, which is today one of the Five Banis and is sung at weddings and on every happy occasion. Where this book says 'Amar Das's own bani', this is its basis.

The count of the shabads — 907 or 869?

The sources differ on the count of Amar Das's shabads — the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism says 907, and some counts give 869. The difference comes from the way of counting — in some counts small pieces are counted separately, in others together. This book writes 907 in the main story, and both counts are recorded here.

The traditional life stories — Janamsakhi and Gurbilas

The stories of Amar Das's life are found in the Janamsakhis and in Gurbilas literature — above all the Mahima Prakash, in which the story of Akbar's visit is found. These were written decades and centuries after Amar Das's death, and in them history and tradition are mixed. In this book every story of the tradition is told as 'the tradition tells us' and made plain in its own note.

Modern scholarship

The dates and events in this book have been checked against the work of modern scholars — J.S. Grewal, 'The Sikhs of the Punjab'; W.H. McLeod, 'The Sikhs — History, Religion and Society'; Max Arthur Macauliffe, 'The Sikh Religion', volume 2; and the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (Punjabi University, Patiala). Where scholars and the tradition say different things, both are recorded in the book.

One plain thing

This book does not show Amar Das as against any religion. He questioned the customs of Hindu society — sati, purdah, caste — but he loved Hindus; he was himself a Vaishnav devotee. His message was not to divide, but to join.

The End · · THE END

The story is complete — but Amar Das's service is not yet over.
